0: The last days of August.... Autumn was already at hand.
1: The sun was setting. A sudden downpour of rain, without thunder or lightning, had just passed rapidly over our wide plain.
2: The garden in front of the house glowed and steamed, all filled with the fire of the sunset and the deluge of rain.
3: She was sitting at a table in the drawing-room, and, with persistent dreaminess, gazing through the half-open door into the garden.
4: I knew what was passing at that moment in her soul; I knew that, after a brief but agonising struggle, she was at that instant giving herself up to a feeling she could no longer master.
6: All at once she got up, went quickly out into the garden, and disappeared.
7:
An hour passed ... a second; she had not returned.

Then I got up, and, getting out of the house, I turned along the walk by which--of that I had no doubt--she had gone.
8: All was darkness about me; the night had already fallen. But on the damp sand of the path a roundish object could be discerned--bright red even through the mist.
9: I stooped down. It was a fresh, new-blown rose. Two hours before I had seen this very rose on her bosom.
10: I carefully picked up the flower that had fallen in the mud, and, going back to the drawing-room, laid it on the table before her chair.
11: And now at last she came back, and with light footsteps, crossing the whole room, sat down at the table.
12: Her face was both paler and more vivid; her downcast eyes, that looked somehow smaller, strayed rapidly in happy confusion from side to side.
13: She saw the rose, snatched it up, glanced at its crushed, muddy petals, glanced at me, and her eyes, brought suddenly to a standstill, were bright with tears.
15:
‘What are you crying for?’ I asked.

‘Why, see this rose. Look what has happened to it.’
16:
Then I thought fit to utter a profound remark.

‘Your tears will wash away the mud,’ I pronounced with a significant expression.
17: ‘Tears do not wash, they burn,’ she answered. And turning to the hearth she flung the rose into the dying flame.
18: ‘Fire burns even better than tears,’ she cried with spirit; and her lovely eyes, still bright with tears, laughed boldly and happily.
19: I saw that she too had been in the fire.
